hook.text: Week six builds a model out of tiny units. Each one does the simplest thing there is: multiply, then add.

unit.text: This is a perceptron. Inputs x one and x two come in, and every connection has a weight.

sum.text: Multiply each input by its weight, add them up, and that sum is the output.

bias.text: There is one more input, x zero, which is always one. Its weight, w zero, is the bias.

tq.text: The slides write all of this as w transpose x. So what does transpose mean?

t1.text: In the slides, vectors are columns. Transpose turns a column into a row. Here, w is minus one point five, one, and one.

t2.text: A row times a column pairs the entries: first with first, second with second, third with third. Multiply each pair.

t3.text: Add the products. Minus one point five, plus one, plus one, is zero point five. A row times a column is always one number: the weighted sum.

whyb.text: So why do we need the bias?

reg.text: For regression, the unit draws a line: y equals w x plus w zero. w sets the slope. w zero moves the whole line up or down.

nob.text: Take the bias away, and every line must pass through the origin, whatever the data look like.

and.text: For classification, the unit outputs one when the sum is above zero. Keep both weights at one, and set the bias to minus one point five.

and2.text: The boundary is the line x one plus x two equals one point five. Only the corner one, one is above it. That is AND.

or.text: Now change only the bias, to minus zero point five. The line slides down, and three corners are above it. That is OR.

shift.text: Same weights, different bias. The weights choose the direction of the line. The bias chooses where it sits. That is bias shifting.

ex1.text: A perceptron outputs the weighted sum.

ex2.text: Transpose turns a column into a row.

ex3.text: w transpose x is one number.

ex4.text: Without a bias, the line must pass through the origin.

ex5.text: AND and OR differ only in the bias.
